claims.text: Combining ab initio-trained machine-learned interatomic potentials with enhanced sampling can substantially reduce the cost of calculating fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The hybrid approach can retain fidelity to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The proposed method applies to multicomponent high-entropy alloys or compounds in both solid and liquid phases.
Machine-learned interatomic potentials should be trained on ab initio data.
Enhanced sampling should be integrated with the trained potentials to calculate solid- and liquid-phase free energies and entropy terms.
The method is applicable to systems containing up to six elements.
The method is applicable from 0.5 to 1.5 times the melting temperature.
Ab initio-trained machine-learned interatomic potentials can capture vibrational entropy and anharmonicity.
The machine-learned interatomic potentials can capture electron–vibration coupling effects.
Machine-learned potentials reduce the computational cost of evaluating interatomic interactions while retaining ab initio accuracy.
Enhanced sampling accelerates free-energy convergence by efficiently exploring phase space in high-temperature and phase-transition regimes.
The hybrid approach will provide a 10–50-fold speedup over explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The hybrid approach will predict free energies and entropies to within 5% of ab initio benchmarks.
Accuracy and speed gains will diminish for systems containing more than six components because the MLIP training data may become insufficient.
Accuracy and speed gains will diminish above 1.5 times the melting temperature because the MLIP training data may become insufficient.

The method can be decisively tested by comparing solid and liquid free energies, fusion enthalpy and entropy, transition temperature, and computational cost against explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
